title: Parameter Estimation
description: Estimators and their properties, maximum likelihood, Fisher information, Bayesian and MAP estimation.
overview: A model has parameters, such as the bias of a coin, the mean and variance of a measurement or the weights of a regression. Data are generated by the model, and we see only a finite sample. Estimation is the problem of inferring the parameters from that sample. An estimator is a rule that does it, and because the sample is random, so is the estimate. We judge an estimator by the distribution of its errors over possible samples: its bias, its variance and its mean squared error.

Two principles dominate. Maximum likelihood picks the parameter that makes the observed data most probable. Bayesian estimation combines the likelihood with a prior and returns the posterior. Both underlie the loss functions and regularizers of the Machine Learning book.
objectives: Compute the bias, variance and mean squared error of an estimator, and explain consistency.
Derive maximum likelihood estimates for the Bernoulli, Gaussian, Poisson and exponential models.
Explain why the sample variance divides by n − 1.
Compute the Fisher information and use it for standard errors and the Cramér–Rao bound.
Derive MAP and posterior estimates for a Gaussian mean and relate them to regularization.

sections.title: Estimators, bias and variance
terms: mean squared error of an estimator
body: Suppose you want the average height of all adults in a city, but you can only measure 50 of them. The average of your 50 is your best guess. A different group of 50 would give a slightly different guess. An estimator is the recipe (here, "average the sample"), and the quality of the recipe is judged by how its answers behave across many possible samples: do they center on the truth (low bias), and how widely do they scatter (variance)? An **estimator** θ̂ = θ̂(X₁, …, X_n) is a function of the sample that is used to guess a parameter θ. Its value for a particular sample is an **estimate**. Since the sample is random, θ̂ is a random variable with its own distribution, the sampling distribution. Three summaries describe its quality:

body: The decomposition MSE = Bias² + Var is the bias–variance decomposition of the Machine Learning book, applied to the estimator. An estimator is **consistent** if θ̂ → θ in probability as n → ∞ (by the law of large numbers, the sample mean is consistent for the mean). **Efficiency** compares variances: among unbiased estimators, the one with the smallest variance is the most efficient.
For i.i.d. data with mean μ and variance σ², the natural estimate of σ² is the average squared deviation from the sample mean. It is biased:

Deviations are measured from X̄, which is itself fitted to the same data and sits closer to the points than μ does. A short calculation shows Σ(X_i − X̄)² = Σ(X_i − μ)² − n(X̄ − μ)², whose expectation is nσ² − σ² = (n − 1)σ². Dividing by n − 1 (**Bessel's correction**) gives an unbiased estimator:

example.title: Two variance estimates
example.problem: The data are 2, 4, 6. Compute the average squared deviation and the unbiased estimate.
example.solution: X̄ = 4 and Σ(x − 4)² = 4 + 0 + 4 = 8. Dividing by n = 3 gives 2.667, and by n − 1 = 2 gives 4. The correction matters most for small n: one point alone (n = 1) gives zero spread, which is clearly too small, and s² is undefined.

body.note: Unbiased does not mean best. Biased estimators can have lower MSE: dividing by n + 1 instead of n − 1 minimizes the mean squared error of the variance estimate of a Gaussian, and shrinkage estimators such as ridge regression accept bias to reduce variance (see the shrinkage example in Generalization).

sections.title: Maximum likelihood estimation
body: You flip a coin 10 times and get 7 heads. Which bias p of the coin makes that result most likely? If p = 0.5, seeing 7 heads is plausible but not common. If p = 0.7, it is the most typical thing to see. If p = 0.1, it would be extremely unlikely. Maximum likelihood chooses the value of p that makes the data you actually saw as probable as possible, here p = 0.7. Given data x₁, …, x_n assumed i.i.d. from a model p(x; θ), the **likelihood** of θ is the probability (density) of the observed data viewed as a function of θ:

body.eq: L(θ) = Π_i p(x_i; θ),    ℓ(θ) = ln L(θ) = Σ_i ln p(x_i; θ)

body: The **maximum likelihood estimator** is θ̂ = argmax L(θ) = argmax ℓ(θ). It chooses the parameter under which the data are least surprising. The recipe: write the log-likelihood, differentiate, set to zero, and check that it is a maximum.

example.title: Bernoulli
example.problem: In n trials there are k successes. Find the MLE of p.
example.solution: ℓ(p) = k ln p + (n − k) ln(1 − p). Setting ℓ′ = k/p − (n − k)/(1 − p) = 0 gives p̂ = k/n, the sample proportion. For 30 heads in 100 flips, p̂ = 0.3.

example.title: Gaussian
example.problem: Find the MLE of μ and σ² for data from N(μ, σ²).
solution: ∂ℓ/∂μ = Σ(x_i − μ)/σ² = 0 gives μ̂ = x̄. ∂ℓ/∂σ² = −n/(2σ²) + Σ(x_i − μ)²/(2σ⁴) = 0 gives σ̂² = (1/n)Σ(x_i − x̄)².

The MLE of the mean is the sample mean. The MLE of the variance divides by n and so is biased: that is why the n − 1 version is used when unbiasedness matters, though the MLE is consistent and the difference vanishes for large n.

example.title: Exponential and Poisson
example.problem: Find the MLE for the rate of an exponential distribution from the data 1, 2, 3, 6, and for the mean of a Poisson distribution from the counts 2, 3, 1, 4.
example.solution: Exponential: ℓ(λ) = n ln λ − λΣx_i, giving λ̂ = n/Σx_i = 1/x̄ = 1/3. Poisson: ℓ(λ) = Σ(x_i ln λ − λ) + const gives λ̂ = x̄ = 2.5.

list: **Consistent**: θ̂ → θ as n → ∞, under mild regularity conditions.
**Asymptotically normal and efficient**: for large n, θ̂ ≈ N(θ, 1/(nI(θ))), where I(θ) is the Fisher information (next section), and no consistent estimator has a smaller asymptotic variance.
**Invariant**: the MLE of g(θ) is g(θ̂). For example the MLE of the standard deviation is √σ̂².
**Often biased in finite samples**, as for σ̂².

Many ML objectives are negative log-likelihoods: squared error (Gaussian noise), cross-entropy (Bernoulli or categorical), and Poisson loss. When no closed form exists (logistic regression, mixtures), the likelihood is maximized numerically by gradient methods, Newton's method or EM.
**Equivalence with KL minimization**: maximizing the average log-likelihood is the same as minimizing KL(p_data ‖ p_θ), up to a constant (see Information Theory).

sections.title: Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound
body: Picture the log-likelihood as a hill whose top is the best estimate. If the hill is a sharp peak, nearby values of θ are much less likely, so the data pin the parameter down tightly. If the hill is a broad, flat dome, many values of θ fit the data about equally well, and the estimate is uncertain. Fisher information is the number that measures how sharp the peak is. How accurately can a parameter be estimated? The answer depends on how sharply the log-likelihood peaks. The **score** is the derivative of the log-likelihood of one observation, ∂ ln p(x; θ)/∂θ. Its mean is zero, and its variance is the **Fisher information**:

body.eq: I(θ) = E[ (∂ ln p(X; θ)/∂θ)² ] = −E[ ∂² ln p(X; θ)/∂θ² ]

body: The second form says that information is the expected curvature of the log-likelihood: a sharply peaked likelihood (high curvature) pins θ down precisely. The **Cramér–Rao bound** states that any unbiased estimator from n observations has
and the MLE attains this bound asymptotically, so its standard error is about 1/√(nI(θ̂)).

example.title: Information of a Bernoulli
example.problem: Find I(p) for a Bernoulli(p) observation, and the standard error of p̂ from n = 100 flips with 30 heads.
example.solution: ln p(x; p) = x ln p + (1 − x) ln(1 − p). The second derivative is −x/p² − (1 − x)/(1 − p)², with expectation −1/p − 1/(1 − p) = −1/(p(1 − p)). So I(p) = 1/(p(1 − p)). Then Var(p̂) ≥ p(1 − p)/n, which the sample proportion attains. With p̂ = 0.3 the standard error is √(0.21/100) = 0.0458, giving the 95% interval 0.3 ± 0.09.

example.title: Information of a Gaussian mean
example.problem: For N(μ, σ²) with known σ², find I(μ) and compare the CR bound with Var(X̄).
example.solution: ln p = −(x − μ)²/(2σ²) + const, so the second derivative is −1/σ² and I(μ) = 1/σ². The bound is σ²/n, which equals Var(X̄): the sample mean is an efficient estimator.

body: For several parameters I(θ) is a matrix, the expected Hessian of the negative log-likelihood, and the covariance of the MLE is approximately (nI(θ))⁻¹. The same matrix appears in natural gradient descent and in the Laplace approximation to the posterior (see Bayesian Methods). In practice, replace I(θ) by the observed information, the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at θ̂. This is how standard errors of logistic regression coefficients are obtained.

sections.title: MAP and Bayesian estimation
body: The Bayesian approach treats θ as random with a prior p(θ). After seeing the data the posterior is p(θ | x) ∝ p(x | θ)p(θ). Point estimates from it include the **MAP** estimate (the posterior mode) and the posterior mean, which minimizes expected squared error.
The log-prior acts as a penalty added to the log-likelihood: a Gaussian prior gives an L2 penalty (ridge) and a Laplace prior gives L1 (lasso), as derived in Regularization.

example.title: Posterior for a Gaussian mean
example.problem: Observations x₁, …, x_n ~ N(μ, σ²) with known σ² = 1. The prior is μ ~ N(0, τ²) with τ² = 1. For n = 4 and sample mean x̄ = 2, find the posterior.
solution: Precisions (inverse variances) add: posterior precision = n/σ² + 1/τ² = 4 + 1 = 5, so the posterior variance is 0.2.
The posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the data mean and the prior mean: (4 · 2 + 1 · 0)/5 = 1.6.

Compare the MLE x̄ = 2: the prior pulls the estimate toward 0, by the fraction 1/5. With n = 100 the weights would be 100:1, and the posterior mean 1.98, almost the MLE. In general the posterior mean is (n/σ²)x̄ + (1/τ²)μ₀ divided by (n/σ² + 1/τ²).

example.title: Laplace smoothing as MAP
example.problem: With a Beta(2, 2) prior and k = 0 successes in n = 3 trials, compare the MLE and the MAP estimate of p.
example.solution: MLE = 0/3 = 0, which says that success is impossible: a harmful conclusion from three trials. MAP = (k + α − 1)/(n + α + β − 2) = (0 + 1)/(3 + 2) = 0.2. Add-one smoothing in naive Bayes corresponds to a Beta(2, 2) prior (add one imaginary success and one failure).

list: With plenty of data the prior washes out and MAP ≈ MLE ≈ posterior mean.
With few data, a sensible prior stabilizes the estimate: it is regularization.
The full posterior gives uncertainty, a credible interval for θ, without asymptotic arguments (see Bayesian Methods).

Frequentist and Bayesian answers can differ in interpretation: a 95% confidence interval is a procedure that covers the true value in 95% of repeated samples, while a 95% credible interval has posterior probability 0.95 of containing θ.

quiz.q: An estimator has bias −0.4 and variance 0.09. What is its mean squared error?
quiz.why: MSE = bias² + variance = 0.16 + 0.09 = 0.25. Adding the bias unsquared would give 0.49, which is wrong.

quiz.q: The observations are 1, 3, 5, 7. What is the unbiased estimate s² of the variance?
quiz.why: The mean is 4 and the squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 9, summing to 20. Dividing by n − 1 = 3 gives 6.67; dividing by n = 4 would give the biased value 5.

quiz.q: Why does (1/n) Σ (Xᵢ − X̄)² underestimate σ² on average?
quiz.a: X̄ is fitted to the same sample, so the points lie closer to X̄ than to the true mean μ
wrong: X̄ is a biased estimator of μ
quiz.why: Σ(Xᵢ − X̄)² = Σ(Xᵢ − μ)² − n(X̄ − μ)², which has expectation (n − 1)σ². X̄ itself is unbiased, and the independence assumption holds.

quiz.q: To estimate a population mean μ, a statistician uses only the first observation X₁ and ignores the rest. This estimator is
quiz.why: E[X₁] = μ, so there is no bias. But its variance stays σ² however large the sample becomes, so it does not converge to μ.

quiz.q: Which statement about unbiased estimators is correct?
quiz.a: A biased estimator can have a smaller mean squared error than an unbiased one
wrong: An unbiased estimator always has the smallest mean squared error
Bias and variance cannot both be positive for a consistent estimator
Shrinkage estimators such as ridge regression are unbiased
quiz.why: MSE = bias² + variance, so accepting a little bias can remove more variance than it costs. Ridge regression does exactly this.

quiz.q: Which statement about the likelihood L(θ) is correct?
quiz.a: It is the probability (density) of the observed data viewed as a function of θ, and it need not integrate to 1 over θ
wrong: It is the probability that the true parameter equals θ
It always integrates to 1 over θ
It is defined only for continuous data
quiz.why: The likelihood fixes the data and varies θ. It is not a distribution over θ; turning it into one requires a prior and Bayes' rule.

quiz.q: The observed waiting times are 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5 minutes, modeled as exponential. What is the MLE of the rate λ?
quiz.why: λ̂ = n/Σxᵢ = 4/8 = 0.5. The sample mean 2 estimates the mean wait 1/λ, not the rate.

quiz.q: For the data 1, 2, 3, 6 assumed Gaussian, what is the maximum likelihood estimate of the standard deviation σ?
quiz.why: The mean is 3 and the squared deviations sum to 14. The MLE of σ² divides by n: 14/4 = 3.5, and by invariance the MLE of σ is its square root.

quiz.q: A classifier is trained by minimizing cross-entropy. This is maximum likelihood under which model of the labels?
quiz.why: The negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli or categorical labels is the cross-entropy. Gaussian noise gives squared error, and Poisson counts give the Poisson loss.

quiz.q: Maximizing the average log-likelihood of the data over θ is equivalent to minimizing, up to a constant,
wrong: the squared distance between p_θ and p_data
quiz.why: The average log-likelihood estimates E_data[ln p_θ], and KL(p_data ‖ p_θ) equals the constant E_data[ln p_data] minus that term. The reversed KL has a different minimizer.

quiz.q: A coin lands heads in 200 of 400 flips. What is the standard error of p̂, using the Fisher information of a Bernoulli?
quiz.why: I(p) = 1/(p(1 − p)) = 4 at p = 0.5, so SE = 1/√(nI) = 1/√1600 = 0.025. The value 0.0006 is the variance, not the standard error.

quiz.q: n = 25 observations come from N(μ, 16) with σ² = 16 known. By the Cramér–Rao bound, what is the smallest possible variance of an unbiased estimator of μ?
quiz.why: I(μ) = 1/σ², so the bound is 1/(nI) = σ²/n = 16/25 = 0.64. The sample mean attains it. The value 0.8 is its standard deviation.

quiz.q: The Cramér–Rao bound says that an unbiased estimator of θ from n i.i.d. observations has variance at least
quiz.why: More information (a sharper log-likelihood peak) and more data both lower the bound, so I(θ) and n appear in the denominator together.

quiz.q: Which Bayesian point estimate minimizes the expected squared error under the posterior?
quiz.why: The mean minimizes squared error, as for any distribution. The median minimizes absolute error, and the MAP is the mode, which can differ from both.

quiz.q: Observations ~ N(μ, 2), n = 6, sample mean 4. The prior is μ ~ N(1, 0.5). What is the posterior mean?
quiz.why: The data precision is n/σ² = 3 and the prior precision is 1/0.5 = 2. The posterior mean is (3·4 + 2·1)/5 = 2.8, with the larger weight on the data. Swapping the weights gives 2.2, and a plain average gives 2.5.

quiz.q: A Beta(2, 2) prior is used for a coin, and 4 heads appear in 5 flips. What is the MAP estimate of the heads probability?
quiz.why: MAP = (k + α − 1)/(n + α + β − 2) = (4 + 1)/(5 + 2) = 5/7. The value 4/5 is the MLE, and 2/3 is the posterior mean.

quiz.q: Which statement correctly describes a 95% confidence interval?
quiz.a: It comes from a procedure that covers the true value in 95% of repeated samples
wrong: Given this data, θ lies in this interval with probability 0.95
95% of the observations lie inside it
It is the central 95% of the prior distribution
quiz.why: In the frequentist view θ is fixed and the interval is random. The statement about the probability that θ lies in the observed interval describes a Bayesian credible interval.

summary: An estimator is a function of the sample, with bias E[θ̂] − θ, variance and MSE = bias² + variance. Consistency means convergence to θ as n grows. The sample variance divides by n − 1 to be unbiased.
Maximum likelihood: θ̂ = argmax Σ ln p(x_i; θ). Bernoulli: k/n; Gaussian: x̄ and (1/n)Σ(x − x̄)²; Poisson: x̄; exponential: 1/x̄. It is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient.
Fisher information I(θ) = −E[∂² ln p/∂θ²] gives the Cramér–Rao bound Var ≥ 1/(nI(θ)) and standard errors. For the Bernoulli I = 1/(p(1 − p)).

Bayesian estimation multiplies the likelihood by a prior. MAP adds ln p(θ) to the log-likelihood: Gaussian prior = ridge, Laplace prior = lasso, Beta prior = smoothing. For a Gaussian mean, precisions add and the posterior mean is precision-weighted.
Many machine learning losses are negative log-likelihoods, so training is maximum likelihood or MAP estimation.

problems.q: Data 3, 5, 10, 14, 18. Compute the sample mean, the MLE of the variance and the unbiased variance.
Find the MLE of θ for the uniform distribution on [0, θ] from the sample 2.1, 0.8, 1.7, 1.2. Is it biased?
problems.solution: L(θ) = θ⁻ⁿ for θ ≥ max x_i and 0 otherwise. It is decreasing in θ, so the maximum is at the smallest allowed value, θ̂ = max x_i = 2.1. It is biased low, since the maximum of the sample is below θ: E[max] = nθ/(n + 1).

problems.q: A Poisson rate is estimated from n = 50 independent counts with sample mean 3.2. The Fisher information for a Poisson is I(λ) = 1/λ. Give the standard error of λ̂ and a 95% interval.
Prior μ ~ N(10, 4) and n = 9 observations with σ² = 9 and sample mean 12. Find the posterior mean and variance.
problems.solution: Data precision n/σ² = 1, prior precision 1/4 = 0.25. Posterior precision = 1.25, so variance 0.8. Posterior mean = (1 × 12 + 0.25 × 10)/1.25 = 14.5/1.25 = 11.6.

problems.q: Show that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of μ and compute its variance.
problems.solution: E[X̄] = (1/n)ΣE[X_i] = μ. By independence Var(X̄) = (1/n²)Σσ² = σ²/n.
